title: Morse Functions: Critical Points To Reeb Graphs
notes: Open by naming the provenance wrinkle: the manifest uses Morse Theory while the PDF chapter title is Morse Functions. The lecture treats that mismatch as useful, because the chapter is really about using well-behaved functions as instruments for reading topology. Emphasize that every visual here is original and every theorem is being used as a computational habit.

title: Learning Arc
notes: Use the arc as the contract for the hour. The students should first trust the local classifier, then understand why sublevel sets are unchanged away from critical values, then see how cell attachments and gradient flow convert geometry into algebra. The last two stops explain why the smooth story matters for PL data and Reeb graphs.

title: Torus Height Sweep
notes: The torus example should feel like the whole chapter in miniature. Below the minimum there is nothing, then a disk appears, then two saddles add one-cells, and the maximum caps the surface. Read the four critical points as the vector c equals (1,2,1), matching the Betti vector beta equals (1,2,1).

title: Critical Point Classifier
notes: Slow down at the Hessian. The first derivative finds candidates, but the second derivative decides whether the candidate is Morse and what index it has. In dimension two, determinant positive with positive trace gives a minimum, determinant negative gives a saddle, and determinant positive with negative trace gives a maximum.

title: Morse Lemma Normal Forms
notes: The Morse lemma is the local straightening theorem for this chapter. After a coordinate change, a nondegenerate critical point has no hidden higher-order behavior nearby. The index is simply the number of negative square terms, so crossing the critical value adds exactly the cell dimension predicted by the local model.

title: Failure Modes
notes: This warning slide separates genericity from wishful drawing. A cubic flat point has a vanishing Hessian, the multi-saddle has too many sectors meeting at one point, equal critical values make two events happen at once, and a sideways torus can have critical circles instead of isolated points. These are precisely the cases the clean theory refuses.

title: Cell Attachment
notes: The attachment theorem is the topological payload of the Morse lemma. Between regular values nothing changes up to diffeomorphism; across one index q critical point, the sublevel set gains a q-cell up to homotopy. The point is not the literal shape of the neighborhood but the dimension of the handle it contributes.

title: Gradient Flow
notes: Gradient flow gives a dynamic way to organize the same sweep. Integral lines climb the function, so on a compact manifold they limit from one critical point to another. Stable and unstable manifolds group together all points with the same future or past endpoint, setting up the cell decomposition used by Morse-Smale theory.

title: Morse-Smale Condition
notes: The extra Morse-Smale hypothesis is about intersections behaving like transverse crossings rather than accidental shared paths. If stable and unstable manifolds meet transversally, cell boundaries are made from lower-dimensional cells. Without it, a saddle-to-saddle trajectory can make a stable manifold boundary miss the complex structure we want.

title: Morse Inequalities
notes: Present the inequalities as an audit of any proposed critical-point inventory. The weak inequalities say each index count must cover the corresponding Betti number, while the strong inequalities include the alternating partial sums. For the torus height function, the counts and Betti numbers match exactly, and both Euler computations give zero.

title: Morse-Smale-Witten Complex
notes: The chain complex replaces cells by critical points and replaces geometric boundary by counting connecting flowlines, here over Z2. The tilted torus has one generator in dimension zero, two in dimension one, and one in dimension two. In the symmetric count shown here, each relevant connection appears twice, so the boundary maps vanish mod two.

title: PL Lower-Star Filtration
notes: This is the algorithmic bridge. A generic PL function orders vertices, and every simplex enters when its highest vertex enters. The closed lower star is the batch of simplices added at that vertex, glued along the lower link. The nested complexes K0 through Kn model the homotopy type of the continuous sublevel sets.

title: PL Critical Vertices
notes: The lower link classifier is the PL replacement for the Hessian. Empty lower link means a new component, two lower-link components mean a one-cell saddle, and a full lower-link circle means a two-cell cap on a surface. Regular vertices have homologically trivial lower links, so they do not change homology.

title: Unfolding + Mayer-Vietoris
notes: A PL multi-saddle shows why PL Morse functions are not simply guaranteed by tiny perturbation. In two dimensions it can be unfolded locally into simple saddles by adding nearby vertices. The Mayer-Vietoris proof then tracks whether the new lower-link cycle creates a class in the current dimension or kills one in the previous dimension.

title: Reeb Graph Definition
notes: The Reeb graph changes the viewpoint from sublevel sets to level-set components. Collapse each contour to a point, keep the induced height map, and the result is a one-dimensional summary of how contours are born, merge, split, and die. It preserves connected components and cannot have more independent graph loops than the original space has one-dimensional homology.

title: Reeb Graph Algorithm + Loop Lemma
notes: Close by tying the smooth and PL stories together. The Reeb graph algorithm sweeps vertices, updates cyclic contour lists, and records nodes for minima, saddles, regular reconnects, and maxima. For connected orientable surfaces, the loop lemma says the cycle rank of a Morse Reeb graph is the genus, so the torus case correctly reports one loop.
